title: STA 2310 Data Communication with AI
text:
Introduction
These are the course notes for STA 2310: Data Communication with AI.
The course focuses on communicating data-driven insight through writing, visualization, presentation, reproducible workflows, and responsible use of artificial intelligence tools. The notes are written for reading before class. Class time will build from these ideas through discussion, workshop activities, peer review, and project work.
Prerequisites: None.

Course Description:
Students will learn to craft evidence-based data stories for specific audiences. The course combines data journalism, technical writing, visualization, accessibility, reproducible research practices, and AI literacy. AI tools will be used as assistants for brainstorming, drafting, summarizing, coding, critique, and revision, but students remain responsible for verifying outputs, documenting assistance, and making final communication choices.
crumbs: Introduction

title: 1  What Is Data Communication with AI?
text:
1.1 The point of the course
Data rarely speaks for itself. A spreadsheet, model output, graph, or dashboard can contain useful evidence, but someone still has to decide what question matters, what comparison is fair, what context the audience needs, and what action the evidence supports.
That work is data communication. It is the practice of turning data into a clear, honest, audience-aware message.
In this course, we will treat data communication as more than making a nice graph or writing a polished paragraph. A strong data communication product connects four things:
AI tools can help at many points in that process. They can suggest wording, summarize a messy draft, explain code, generate alternative chart ideas, or act like a first-pass reviewer. But AI tools can also invent details, smooth over uncertainty, reproduce bias, misunderstand context, or make weak claims sound confident.
So the central habit of the course is simple:
You may ask AI tools for help. You may not hand your judgment to them.

title: 1  What Is Data Communication with AI?
section: 1.2 What counts as a data story?
text:
1.2 What counts as a data story?
A data story is not necessarily dramatic. It does not need a hero, a villain, or a twist ending. In this class, a data story is a claim about the world supported by data and shaped for a particular audience.
For example:

A campus office wants to know when tutoring demand is highest.
A public health group wants to explain why a rate changed over time.
A sports analyst wants to show whether a team improved after a roster change.
A nonprofit wants donors to understand which need is growing fastest.
A city department wants residents to understand a budget tradeoff.

Each example involves data, but the communication problem is different. A campus office may need a concise internal memo. A public health group may need a public-facing explainer. A sports analyst may need a visual comparison. A nonprofit may need a one-page donor brief. A city department may need plain language and careful caveats.
The same dataset can support different products because audiences need different things.






ExampleExample 1.1: Same number, different message



Suppose a dataset shows that 38% of students who visited a writing center returned for at least one additional appointment.
That number could be communicated several ways:

To students: “Many students come back after their first visit, which suggests the center is useful beyond one-time proofreading.”
To administrators: “Repeat use may indicate sustained demand; staffing plans should account for students who return across the semester.”
To writing center tutors: “A first appointment often begins an ongoing support relationship, so intake notes and follow-up guidance matter.”

The statistic is the same. The communication changes because the audience and purpose change.

title: 1  What Is Data Communication with AI?
text:
1.4 Responsible use
Responsible AI use in data communication has three parts.
First, protect people and data. Do not paste private, sensitive, confidential, or identifiable data into an AI tool unless the course instructions explicitly say the tool and data are approved for that use. Public datasets can still involve real people, so privacy is not only a technical rule. It is also an ethical habit.
Second, verify outputs. AI tools can produce fluent mistakes. They may invent sources, misread a prompt, write code that runs but answers the wrong question, or suggest a chart that hides the important comparison. Fluency is not evidence.
Third, own the communication. If your name is on the work, you are responsible for the claims, language, code, and design choices. AI can assist with process, but it cannot take responsibility for the final message.
crumbs: 1  What Is Data Communication with AI?

title: 1  What Is Data Communication with AI?
text:
1.5 A first communication checklist
Before you make a graph, write a paragraph, or ask an AI tool for help, pause and answer these questions:

What question am I trying to answer?
Who needs to understand the answer?
What does this audience already know?
What evidence do I have?
What evidence do I still need?
What could be misunderstood?
What should the audience do, think, or ask next?

This checklist will return throughout the course. It is intentionally simple because simple questions catch many complicated mistakes.






ExampleExample 1.2: A weak prompt and a stronger prompt



Weak prompt:

Make this data sound better.

Stronger prompt:

I am writing for first-year college students who may be nervous about asking for academic help. Based on the paragraph below, suggest three clearer ways to explain the main finding. Do not add facts that are not in the paragraph. Point out any claims that need more evidence.

The stronger prompt names the audience, task, constraint, and desired critique. It also tells the AI not to invent facts. That does not guarantee a good answer, but it gives you a better starting point for responsible revision.
crumbs: 1  What Is Data Communication with AI?

text:
1.6 Recap








Keyword
Definition




Data communication
The practice of turning data into a clear, honest, audience-aware message.


Data story
A claim about the world supported by data and shaped for a particular audience.


Audience
The people who need to understand, use, question, or act on the message.


AI collaborator
A tool that can assist with brainstorming, drafting, coding, critique, or revision, while the human remains responsible for judgment.


AI use log
A short record of how AI was used, what changed, and how the final work was verified.


Verification
The process of checking that claims, code, summaries, and visuals are accurate and appropriate.

title: 1  What Is Data Communication with AI?
text:
1.7 Check your understanding






NoteProblems






In your own words, explain the difference between data analysis and data communication.
Suppose an AI tool suggests a more dramatic headline for a chart. What questions should you ask before using it?
Choose one audience for the statistic “38% of students returned for another writing center appointment.” Write one sentence that would make the statistic useful for that audience.
Name one way AI could help with data communication and one way it could create a problem.










TipSolutions






Data analysis focuses on working with data to find patterns, summaries, comparisons, or models. Data communication focuses on explaining evidence clearly to an audience so they can understand, decide, or ask better questions.
Ask whether the headline is accurate, whether it exaggerates the evidence, whether it matches the audience, whether it hides uncertainty, and whether every claim in it can be supported by the data.
Answers will vary. For administrators: “Because more than one-third of students return after an initial appointment, staffing plans should account for repeat visits rather than only first-time demand.”
AI could help by suggesting clearer wording or possible audience questions. It could create a problem by inventing facts, overstating a result, missing context, or making biased language sound polished.

title: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries
text:
2.1 Why audience matters
In many statistics and data science courses, the workflow sounds like this:
That workflow is useful, but it hides one of the most important communication decisions: who is this for?
Audience is not something we sprinkle on at the end. Audience affects which question matters, which evidence is relevant, which words are clear, which caveats need to be stated, and which visual form will help rather than distract.
Suppose a dataset shows that visits to a campus tutoring center peak in the two weeks before midterms. That pattern could matter to several groups:
The evidence is the same, but the communication task is not. A message that works for one audience may be too vague, too technical, too detailed, or too action-oriented for another.
crumbs: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries

title: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries
text:
get the data;
analyze the data;
make a graph;
explain what happened.





Students may need to know that booking early is wise.
Tutors may need to plan for busier shifts.
Administrators may need to allocate staffing.
Faculty may need to coordinate review sessions.
A public audience may need a simple explanation of how academic support is used.








ExampleExample 2.1: Same evidence, different audience



Imagine this finding:

Students who visited the tutoring center at least twice had higher average course grades than students who did not visit.

For students, a reasonable message might be:

Students who use tutoring often do well, and returning for another visit is a normal part of learning.

For administrators, a better message might be:

Repeat tutoring visits are associated with stronger course outcomes, but the data do not show whether tutoring caused the difference; additional study could help evaluate program impact.

The student-facing version encourages help-seeking. The administrator-facing version is more careful about causation because it may affect policy, funding, or assessment.
crumbs: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries

title: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries
text:
2.2 Audience is a decision context
It is tempting to define an audience only by a label: students, faculty, parents, customers, voters, managers, patients, donors, or fans. Labels help, but they are not enough.
A useful audience description includes context:

Need: What problem or question brings this audience to the data?
Knowledge: What do they already understand, and what needs explanation?
Power: What decisions can they make with the information?
Risk: What could happen if they misunderstand the message?
Constraint: What time, attention, or technical background do they have?

For example, “students” is too broad. First-year students choosing whether to visit tutoring are different from senior statistics majors evaluating a data visualization. Both are students, but they need different messages.

Primary and secondary audiences
Many real data products have more than one audience. A public report may be written for community members but also read by journalists, administrators, grant reviewers, and people represented in the data.
When this happens, choose a primary audience. The primary audience is the group whose needs most shape the communication. Secondary audiences still matter, especially for ethics and interpretation, but they should not pull the message in every direction.
If every audience is equally important, the result often becomes mushy: too general for technical readers, too technical for general readers, and not very useful for anyone.


A quick audience profile
Before writing a data claim, try this four-sentence profile:

My primary audience is…
They need to understand…
They may already believe or assume…
The biggest risk if I communicate poorly is…

This profile is short, but it forces useful choices.






ExampleExample 2.2: Audience profile



Suppose you are communicating a chart about student sleep and exam performance.
Audience profile:

My primary audience is first-year college students.
They need to understand that sleep is related to academic performance, but it is not the only factor.
They may already believe that staying up late is a necessary part of college success.
The biggest risk if I communicate poorly is making a correlation sound like a guarantee or making students feel blamed for complicated academic pressures.

That profile points toward a careful message: sleep matters, but the data should not be used to shame students or oversimplify academic success.
crumbs: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries

title: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries
text:
2.3 From topic to claim
A topic is a general area. A claim is a specific statement that can be supported, challenged, revised, or rejected using evidence.
Topic:

Student study habits.

Better question:

How do study hours vary across the semester?

Possible claim:

In this sample, reported study hours increased sharply during the two weeks before midterms.

The claim is more useful because it names:

the group or data source;
the measured quantity;
the direction or pattern;
the time frame.

Good claims are not always bold. Sometimes the strongest claim is cautious:

The available data suggest a possible increase, but missing responses make the size of the change uncertain.

That is still a claim. It tells the audience what the evidence can and cannot support.

Common types of data claims
Different claims require different levels of evidence.









Claim Type
What It Says
Example
Evidence Needed




Descriptive
What was observed
“Forty percent of respondents used tutoring.”
Clear measurement and relevant denominator


Comparative
How groups or times differ
“Use was higher before midterms than after midterms.”
Fair comparison and consistent definitions


Associational
How variables move together
“Tutoring visits were associated with higher grades.”
Attention to confounding and design limits


Causal
One thing produced a change in another
“Tutoring increased grades.”
Strong design, usually experiment or careful causal strategy


Predictive
What is likely to happen
“Visits will likely rise next week.”
Model validation and uncertainty


Evaluative
Whether something is good, bad, enough, or worth doing
“The program should expand.”
Evidence plus values, costs, constraints, and alternatives



One of the most common communication mistakes is using evidence for one claim type while writing as if it supports a stronger claim type.
If your data are descriptive, do not write a causal headline. If your evidence shows an association, do not write as if you proved an intervention worked.
crumbs: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries

title: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries
text:
2.4 The claim ladder
Think of claims as a ladder. Each step requires more evidence than the one below it.

We observed this.
This group differed from that group.
These variables were associated.
This factor likely contributed to that outcome.
This action should be taken.

The higher you climb, the more support you need. A recommendation is not just a statistic with an exclamation point. It requires judgment about consequences, alternatives, cost, uncertainty, and audience needs.






ExampleExample 2.3: Climbing too high



Evidence:

Students who used a study app had higher average exam scores than students who did not.

Careful claim:

In this sample, study app users had higher average exam scores.

Too high on the ladder:

The study app improves exam scores.

Why is the second claim too strong? Students who choose to use a study app may already be more organized, more motivated, or taking different courses. The data may show an association, but the claim uses causal language.
crumbs: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries

title: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries
text:
2.5 Evidence fit
Evidence fit means the evidence matches the claim. This is one of the most important ideas in data communication.
Ask:

Does the evidence directly measure the thing named in the claim?
Is the denominator clear?
Is the comparison fair?
Is the time period appropriate?
Are the categories defined?
Are important groups missing?
Could another explanation fit the same pattern?


Denominators
A percentage without a denominator can mislead.
Consider:

Complaints increased by 50%.

That sounds large. But it means different things depending on the denominator:

from 2 complaints to 3;
from 200 complaints to 300;
from 20,000 complaints to 30,000.

The percentage alone is not enough. Good communication often includes both the rate and the count when the count affects interpretation.


Benchmarks
Many numbers need a comparison point.

The average wait time was 14 minutes.

Is that good or bad? It depends. Compared with what?

last semester?
similar offices?
the office goal?
student expectations?
the time required for the service?

Benchmarks help audiences interpret scale. Without a benchmark, a number may be accurate but not meaningful.


Time frame
Time frame changes interpretation.

Website traffic increased.

Over what period? Compared to what previous period? Was there a holiday, campaign, news event, outage, or seasonal pattern?
Data communication should make time visible when time affects interpretation.


Missing data
Missing data are not just a technical problem. They are a communication problem.
If many students skip a survey question about financial stress, the missingness itself may matter. If a public dataset excludes some neighborhoods, the map may look complete while hiding absence. If an AI tool summarizes a dataset without noticing missing values, it may produce a clean but false story.
When missing data could affect the message, say so.
crumbs: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries

title: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries
text:
2.6 Responsible AI boundaries
AI tools can help with audience adaptation, claim checking, drafting, revision, and critique. But they also make it easier to write beyond the evidence.
A useful way to think about AI use is to divide tasks into green, yellow, and red zones.

Green-zone uses
Green-zone uses are usually appropriate if you still verify the result.

Ask for alternate wording.
Ask for possible audience questions.
Ask for a plain-language explanation of a technical sentence.
Ask for a list of possible caveats.
Ask for a critique of whether a claim sounds causal.
Ask for help debugging code, followed by your own check.

Green-zone uses support thinking. They do not replace it.


Yellow-zone uses
Yellow-zone uses may be appropriate, but they require extra care.

Asking AI to summarize a source or dataset.
Asking AI to recommend a chart type.
Asking AI to rewrite a whole section.
Asking AI to generate code for cleaning or plotting data.
Asking AI to create peer review comments.

These tasks can be helpful, but they can also quietly change the meaning. You need to compare the output against the data, the assignment, and your own intended claim.


Red-zone uses
Red-zone uses are not acceptable in this course unless the instructor gives explicit permission.

Pasting private, sensitive, or identifiable data into an unapproved AI tool.
Letting AI invent sources or citations.
Submitting AI-generated claims you have not checked.
Using AI to hide lack of understanding.
Allowing AI to make the final decision about what the evidence proves.
Presenting AI-generated work as if it involved no AI assistance when it did.

The problem is not that AI was used. The problem is unsupported, undisclosed, or irresponsible use.






ExampleExample 2.4: AI boundary check



Prompt:

Here is my paragraph about tutoring visits and grades. Identify any places where I make a causal claim that the data do not support.

This is a green-zone use. The AI is acting as a reviewer, and the student still decides what to revise.
Prompt:

Here is a file with student names, grades, and tutoring records. Tell me which students are at risk.

This is a red-zone use unless the tool and data handling have been explicitly approved. It involves identifiable student data and could cause harm if mishandled.
crumbs: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries

title: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries
text:
2.7 A practical workflow
When you are preparing a data communication product, use this order:

Name the audience. Write a short audience profile.
State the claim. Make it specific enough to check.
Locate the evidence. Identify the exact data, summary, graph, or comparison that supports the claim.
Check the claim type. Is it descriptive, comparative, associational, causal, predictive, or evaluative?
Look for missing context. Denominator, benchmark, time frame, definitions, and missing data.
Use AI carefully. Ask AI to help revise, critique, or brainstorm, but do not let it determine truth.
Document AI use. Record what helped, what you changed, and how you verified the final result.

This workflow is slower than copying a chart into a slide and writing the first sentence that comes to mind. It is also how you avoid many of the mistakes that make data communication misleading.
crumbs: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries

title: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries
text:
2.8 Recap








Keyword
Definition




Audience
The people who need to understand, use, question, or act on the message.


Primary audience
The audience whose needs most shape the communication.


Claim
A specific statement that can be supported, challenged, revised, or rejected using evidence.


Evidence fit
The match between what the evidence shows and what the claim says.


Claim ladder
The idea that stronger claims, especially causal or action claims, require stronger evidence.


Denominator
The total or reference group used to interpret a count, rate, or percentage.


Benchmark
A comparison point that helps an audience understand whether a number is large, small, typical, or unusual.


Responsible AI boundary
A limit on AI use based on privacy, verification, attribution, evidence, and human responsibility.

title: 2  Audience, Claims, Evidence, and AI Boundaries
text:
2.9 Check your understanding






NoteProblems






Why is “students” usually too broad to be a complete audience description?
Classify each claim as descriptive, comparative, associational, causal, predictive, or evaluative:

“In this sample, 42% of students used tutoring at least once.”
“Tutoring users had higher average grades than non-users.”
“Tutoring improved student grades.”
“The university should expand tutoring hours.”

A report says, “Complaints increased by 50%.” What additional information would help you interpret that claim?
Explain why this AI revision is risky:
Original: “Students who used the study app had higher average exam scores, but the data do not show whether the app caused the difference.”
AI revision: “The study app helped students earn higher exam scores.”
Give one green-zone AI use, one yellow-zone AI use, and one red-zone AI use for this course.










TipSolutions






“Students” is too broad because students differ in background knowledge, needs, decisions, constraints, and risks. First-year students deciding whether to seek tutoring need a different message than student government leaders reviewing a campus report.

Descriptive. b. Comparative or associational, depending on the surrounding context. c. Causal. d. Evaluative or recommendation.

You would want the original count and new count, the denominator or population, the time frame, whether reporting procedures changed, and whether the increase is large relative to normal variation.
The revision changes an association into a causal claim. The original says app users had higher scores but warns that the data do not prove causation. The AI revision removes that caveat and implies the app produced the improvement.
Answers will vary. Green-zone: asking AI to identify vague language in a draft. Yellow-zone: asking AI to summarize a dataset or rewrite a section, followed by careful verification. Red-zone: pasting identifiable student data into an unapproved AI tool or submitting AI-generated claims without checking them.

title: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio
text:
3.1 The basic idea
Data communication is not only about choosing the right words or making a good chart. It is also about creating a workflow that helps you make, revise, check, and share your work.
In this course, we will use Quarto for many written and visual products. Quarto lets you write one source file and render it into polished outputs such as HTML pages, PDF documents, Word documents, slides, websites, and books. That means your writing, code, tables, figures, equations, and notes can live together in one reproducible file.
This chapter introduces the basic model. You do not need to master every option today. You do need to understand what a Quarto file is, how RStudio renders it, and what can go wrong when the same source is sent to different output formats.
A Quarto source file usually ends in .qmd. The .qmd file is the file you edit. The rendered file is the file your audience reads.

title: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio
crumbs: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio

title: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio
text:
3.2 RStudio as the authoring environment
We will assume you are using RStudio.
In RStudio, you can create a new Quarto file by going to File > New File > Quarto Document. RStudio will ask for a title and an output format. For your first few documents, HTML is usually the easiest output because it renders quickly and is forgiving.
RStudio has two useful editing modes:

Source mode, where you see the raw Quarto markdown.
Visual mode, where RStudio gives you a document-like editing interface.

You may use either mode. Source mode helps you learn the structure. Visual mode can be helpful for tables, links, images, citations, and equation editing. Even when you use Visual mode, it is worth switching to Source mode sometimes so you can see what RStudio created.
To render, click the Render button near the top of the editor. If your document has multiple formats, RStudio lets you choose which one to render.
crumbs: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio

title: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio
text:
3.3 The YAML header
Most Quarto files begin with a YAML header. YAML controls document metadata and rendering options.
Here is a minimal Quarto document:
---
title: "My First Quarto Document"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
---
After the YAML header, you write the body of the document:
## Main Finding

The main finding is that visits increased from September to October.

## Evidence

The data came from weekly tutoring center records.
YAML is picky about indentation. If something fails unexpectedly, check for:

tabs instead of spaces;
missing colons;
uneven indentation;
quotation marks that do not close;
a YAML header that starts with --- but does not end with ---.
crumbs: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio

title: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio
section: 3.4 Rendering one document to HTML, PDF, or Word
text:
3.4 Rendering one document to HTML, PDF, or Word
A single .qmd file can be rendered to several common formats.
For an HTML page:
---
title: "Tutoring Center Summary"
format: html
---
For a PDF document:
---
title: "Tutoring Center Summary"
format: pdf
---
For a Word document:
---
title: "Tutoring Center Summary"
format: docx
---
You can also list multiple formats in the same file:
---
title: "Tutoring Center Summary"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
  pdf:
    toc: true
  docx:
    toc: true
---
In RStudio, you can choose which format to render. From a terminal, the commands would look like this:
quarto render tutoring-summary.qmd --to html
quarto render tutoring-summary.qmd --to pdf
quarto render tutoring-summary.qmd --to docx
HTML is often best for web reading. PDF is often best for printing or preserving page layout. Word is often best when someone needs to comment, track changes, or edit the file in Microsoft Word.






WarningPDF rendering depends on LaTeX



PDF output often requires a working LaTeX installation. If HTML and Word render but PDF fails, the problem may not be your writing. It may be a missing LaTeX tool, a LaTeX package issue, or math/table/image syntax that PDF handles more strictly.
crumbs: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio

title: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio
section: 3.5 Documents, HTML pages, slides, and books
text:
3.5 Documents, HTML pages, slides, and books
Quarto can create several kinds of communication products. The same basic writing rules apply, but the project structure and output format change.









Product
Usual Source
Common Outputs
Typical Use




Document
One .qmd file
HTML, PDF, Word
Report, memo, analysis, handout


HTML page
One .qmd file rendered to html
HTML
Web page, Canvas page, online notes


Slides
One .qmd file
revealjs HTML, pptx, beamer PDF
Presentation or short talk


Book
A Quarto project with multiple .qmd chapters
HTML, PDF, Word, EPUB
Multi-chapter notes, textbook, manual



The word “document” can be confusing. A Quarto document is the source you write. HTML, PDF, and Word are possible outputs from that source.

HTML documents
HTML is the most web-friendly format. It supports links, responsive layout, search in websites and books, interactive graphics, and embedded media.
A useful HTML setup might look like this:
---
title: "Short Data Report"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
---
HTML is also the format we will often use when preparing material for Canvas or the course book.


PDF documents
PDF is useful when page layout matters. It is also useful when you need a file that will print consistently.
---
title: "Printable Data Report"
format:
  pdf:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
---
PDF is less forgiving than HTML. Very wide tables, huge images, long URLs, and complicated math can overflow the page. If a document renders well to HTML but badly to PDF, inspect the parts that are physically wide.


Word documents
Word output is useful when your audience wants to edit, comment, or use track changes.
---
title: "Editable Data Report"
format:
  docx:
    toc: true
---
Word is not just “HTML in Microsoft Word.” Some layouts, interactive features, web-only styling, and advanced figure arrangements may not transfer exactly. If Word is the final format, always open the .docx file and inspect it.


Slides
Quarto slides are usually written as a .qmd file where headings become slides. The most common HTML slide format is revealjs.
---
title: "Tutoring Center Patterns"
format: revealjs
---

## Main Finding

Tutoring visits increased before midterms.

## Evidence

- Weekly visit counts
- Course support records
- Comparison across four weeks
For PowerPoint:
---
title: "Tutoring Center Patterns"
format: pptx
---
For PDF slides, Quarto can use Beamer:
---
title: "Tutoring Center Patterns"
format: beamer
---
There is an important practical distinction here. Word (docx) is a document format, not a slide format. If someone asks for editable slides, they probably want PowerPoint (pptx), not Word. If someone asks for a printable slide handout, PDF may be the better choice.


Books
A Quarto book is a project made from multiple .qmd files. This course textbook is a Quarto book.
A small book project might look like this:
my-book/
  _quarto.yml
  index.qmd
  01-intro.qmd
  02-analysis.qmd
  03-communication.qmd
The _quarto.yml file controls the book:
project:
  type: book

book:
  title: "My Data Communication Book"
  chapters:
    - index.qmd
    - 01-intro.qmd
    - 02-analysis.qmd
    - 03-communication.qmd

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
  pdf: default
  docx: default
HTML books are useful for course notes because students can navigate by chapter and use search. PDF or Word book output may be useful for printing or review, but those formats can expose layout problems that do not appear in HTML.
crumbs: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio

title: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio
text:
3.6 Including images
Images are central to data communication. Quarto can include common image formats such as .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, and .svg, although support can vary by output format.
A good habit is to create an images folder inside your project:
project-folder/
  report.qmd
  images/
    tutoring-dashboard.png
    campus-photo.jpg
Then include the image with a relative path:
![Weekly tutoring dashboard](images/tutoring-dashboard.png)
The text inside square brackets is the figure caption when the image is treated as a figure. You can also add alt text, size, alignment, and an ID for cross-referencing:
![Weekly tutoring dashboard](images/tutoring-dashboard.png){#fig-tutoring-dashboard fig-alt="A line chart showing tutoring visits increasing before midterms." width="80%"}

As shown in @fig-tutoring-dashboard, visits rose in the weeks before midterms.
Use image formats intentionally:








Format
Works Well For
Watch Out For




.png
Charts, screenshots, diagrams, images with text
File size can be large


.jpg or .jpeg
Photos
Text and chart lines may become blurry


.gif
Simple animation in HTML
Animation may not work in PDF or Word


.svg
Vector graphics in HTML
May need conversion for some PDF or Word workflows


.pdf
Vector figures for PDF output
Not ideal for HTML pages unless converted









ExampleExample 3.2: Choosing an image format



If you export a bar chart from R, .png is usually a good choice because the chart text and bars stay sharp. If you include a photograph of students working in a classroom, .jpg is usually better because it compresses photos efficiently.
If you are rendering to PDF and the image looks blurry, try exporting the plot at a larger size or using a vector format such as .pdf or .svg, depending on the target output.



Common image problems
Image problems are common because an image is an external file. The .qmd file points to the image, but the image itself still has to exist in the right place.
Common problems include:

the path is wrong;
the file extension is wrong, such as .jpeg in the folder but .jpg in the source;
the filename has spaces or inconsistent capitalization;
the image is outside the project folder;
the image is huge and makes the output file too large;
the image is readable on your computer but missing when you share the project.

Use simple filenames:
good: tutoring_dashboard.png
good: campus-photo.jpg
avoid: Screenshot 2027-01-18 at 9.45.22 AM.png
avoid: final FINAL chart (new).jpeg
For accessibility, include meaningful alt text when the image communicates information. Alt text should describe the information a reader would miss if they could not see the image.
Weak alt text:
![](images/chart.png){fig-alt="A chart."}
Better alt text:
![](images/chart.png){fig-alt="A bar chart showing that tutoring visits were highest during the two weeks before midterms."}
crumbs: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio

title: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio
text:
3.7 Writing equations
Quarto supports equations written in LaTeX-style math notation.
Use single dollar signs for inline equations:
The sample proportion is $\hat{p} = x / n$.
Use double dollar signs for display equations:
$$
\hat{p} = \frac{x}{n}
$$
You can label an equation and refer to it later:
$$
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}
$$ {#eq-z-score}

The standardized value in @eq-z-score tells us how far an observation is from the mean in standard deviation units.
Here is the same idea rendered as an equation:
\[
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}
\tag{3.1}\]
The value in Equation 3.1 is useful when we want to communicate how unusual a value is relative to a distribution.

Common equation problems
Equations are powerful, but they also create some predictable problems.
If you are writing about money, the dollar sign can accidentally start math mode. Escape a dollar sign with a backslash:
The program cost \$25 per student.
If your equation has an opening brace {, it usually needs a closing brace }:
\frac{x}{n}
If you render to PDF, math errors may stop the whole render. HTML may appear more forgiving, but a broken equation is still a broken communication product.
For a general audience, do not use equations just because you can. An equation is useful when it clarifies the structure of a calculation. If the audience only needs the idea, a sentence may communicate better.
crumbs: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio

title: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio
text:
3.8 Code chunks and results
Quarto can run R code chunks and include the results in the rendered output.
A basic R chunk looks like this:
line 1: ```{r}
line 2: #| label: simple-mean
line 3:
line 4: scores <- c(82, 88, 91, 77, 85)
line 5: mean(scores)
line 6: ```
When you type this in a real .qmd file, remove the line 1: labels. They are included here only so this textbook can display the chunk structure without running it.
Chunk options let you control what the reader sees:
line 1: ```{r}
line 2: #| label: setup
line 3: #| include: false
line 4:
line 5: library(tidyverse)
line 6: ```
In this example, include: false means the code runs but does not appear in the final document.
For this course, think of code chunks as part of the evidence trail. If a number appears in your report, your Quarto file can show where it came from.

3.11 Recap







Idea
Takeaway




.qmd source
The editable Quarto file where writing, code, images, and equations live.


Rendered output
The file your audience reads, such as HTML, PDF, Word, slides, or a book.


YAML
The document settings at the top of the file.


HTML
Best for web reading, links, search, and interactive or flexible layouts.


PDF
Best for printing and fixed page layout, but stricter about formatting.


Word
Best for editing and comments, but not identical to HTML or PDF.


Slides

title: 3  Getting Started with Quarto in RStudio
text:
3.12 Check your understanding






NoteProblems






What is the difference between a .qmd source file and a rendered output file?
When might HTML be a better output format than PDF?
When might Word be a better output format than HTML?
What output format would you choose for editable slides?
Why is this image path likely to create problems?
![](C:/Users/Me/Downloads/final FINAL chart (new).png)
Write Quarto markdown that includes an image named exam_scores.png from an images folder. Include useful alt text.
What is wrong with this sentence in a Quarto document?
The program costs $25 per student and saves $40 in staff time.
Why should you inspect the rendered output even if the source file looks correct?
How could an AI tool help with Quarto? What would you still need to verify yourself?










TipSolutions






A .qmd file is the editable source file. It contains the writing, YAML settings, code, image links, equations, and other instructions. The rendered output is the file an audience reads, such as .html, .pdf, .docx, a slide deck, or a book page.
HTML may be better than PDF when the document will be read online, shared through a website or Canvas, searched, linked, updated frequently, or used with interactive or responsive content. HTML is also usually easier to troubleshoot while learning Quarto.
Word may be better than HTML when someone needs to edit the document, leave comments, use track changes, or fit the work into an office workflow. It is often a practical format for drafts, reports that need feedback, or documents that will be revised by multiple people.
For editable slides, choose PowerPoint output with format: pptx. If you want HTML slides, use format: revealjs. If you want PDF slides, use format: beamer or print/export HTML slides to PDF, depending on the situation.
The image path is likely to create problems because it points to a personal location on one computer rather than a project-relative path. It also uses a filename with spaces, parentheses, and repeated words, which increases the chance of mistakes. A better workflow is to put the file inside an images folder in the project and use a relative path such as:
![](images/final_chart.png)
One good answer is:
![Exam score distribution](images/exam_scores.png){fig-alt="A chart showing the distribution of exam scores."}
The best alt text depends on what the image actually shows. If the chart shows a specific pattern, the alt text should name that pattern.
The dollar signs may be interpreted as math delimiters rather than currency symbols. Escape currency dollar signs with backslashes:
The program costs \$25 per student and saves \$40 in staff time.
The source file can look correct while the rendered output still has problems. Images may be missing, equations may render incorrectly, tables may overflow, links may break, callouts may display oddly, or Word/PDF output may differ from HTML. The render is the version your audience sees, so it must be checked directly.
An AI tool could help draft a YAML header, explain an error message, suggest Quarto syntax, revise wording, create a starter outline, or identify places where the document may be unclear. You would still need to render the file, inspect the output, verify that syntax and code work, check that images and equations display correctly, and make sure the final communication is accurate for the audience.

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
text:
4.1 Why source choice matters
Before you can communicate with data, you need data worth communicating from.
This sounds obvious, but it is one of the easiest places to make a mistake. A polished chart can hide a weak source. A fluent paragraph can overstate what a dataset actually measures. An AI tool can suggest a dataset that sounds real but does not exist, or summarize a source in a way that skips the most important limitation.
In this chapter, we focus on how to find and evaluate data sources before building a memo, graph, dashboard, or report. The goal is not to find the largest dataset. The goal is to find a source that fits the question, audience, claim, and ethical responsibilities of the communication task.
A data source shapes what can be claimed.
Suppose you want to communicate about student success. Different sources support different claims:
The source does not just provide numbers. It defines the population, time frame, variables, categories, and limits of the evidence.
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
text:
Source
What It Might Support
What It May Not Support




Tutoring center visit logs
Patterns in tutoring use
Whether tutoring caused better grades


End-of-course survey
Student perceptions
Actual learning gains


Registrar course records
Enrollment, grades, completion
Why students struggled or succeeded


Interviews with students
Lived experiences and explanations
Campus-wide percentages


National education dataset
Broad comparisons across institutions
Details about one local program










ExampleExample 4.1: Same topic, different source



Topic: student food insecurity.
A campus survey may help answer:

What percentage of surveyed students reported worrying about food access this semester?

A dining hall transaction dataset may help answer:

How often are meal plan swipes used during each week of the semester?

A local food pantry record may help answer:

How many pantry visits occurred each month?

These are related questions, but they are not interchangeable. The survey, dining hall data, and pantry records measure different things.
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
text:
4.2 Start with a source-seeking question
Do not start with “I need a dataset about education” or “I need data about health.” Those topics are too broad.
Start with a source-seeking question:

Who or what should the data describe?
What measure do I need?
What time period matters?
What level of detail matters?
What comparison or context do I need?
What kind of claim am I hoping to make?

For example:







Broad Topic
Better Source-Seeking Question




College enrollment
What public source reports undergraduate enrollment by institution and year?


Local employment
What official source reports unemployment rates by county and month?


Public health
What source reports county-level health outcomes with definitions and collection notes?


Student support
What campus source records tutoring visits by week and course?



A source-seeking question makes the search more efficient because it names the data structure you need.
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
section: 4.3 What counts as a data source?
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
text:
4.4 Documentation, metadata, and data dictionaries
Three words come up often when evaluating data sources: documentation, metadata, and data dictionary.








Term
What It Usually Means
Why It Matters




Documentation
General explanation of the dataset, collection process, scope, and use
Helps you understand what the dataset can and cannot support


Metadata
Information about the dataset, such as title, owner, date, format, license, and update schedule
Helps you cite, track, and judge the source


Data dictionary
A list of variables, definitions, units, categories, and coding rules
Helps you interpret columns correctly



For this course, do not worry about memorizing technical distinctions. The practical question is:

Can I explain where the data came from, what it means, and what limits it has?

If the answer is no, the source is not ready for communication.
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
text:
4.5 Evaluating a source
Use the following checks before building a claim from a source.

Relevance
Relevance asks whether the source actually fits the question.
Ask:

Does the source describe the group, place, time, or process I care about?
Does it include the measure I need?
Does it include the comparison I want to make?
Does the level of detail fit my audience?

Low relevance creates weak claims. A national dataset may not answer a local campus question. A one-time survey may not answer a trend question. A count may not answer a rate question.


Authority
Authority asks who created or maintains the data.
Ask:

What organization produced the source?
Does the organization have a clear role or expertise related to the data?
Is the source original, or did it copy data from somewhere else?
Is there contact information, citation guidance, or documentation?

Authority does not mean the source is perfect. Official sources can still have limits. But source ownership helps you judge credibility and responsibility.


Collection method
Collection method asks how the data were created.
Ask:

Was the data collected through a survey, administrative record, sensor, transaction system, observation, experiment, or web scrape?
Who was included?
Who may have been missed?
Were responses required or voluntary?
Were definitions consistent over time?

The collection method tells you what kind of evidence the data are.


Definitions and measurement
Definitions ask what the variables mean.
Ask:

How is each key variable defined?
What unit is used?
Are categories mutually exclusive?
Are missing values coded as blanks, zeros, NA, 999, or something else?
Did the definition change over time?

A variable name is not enough. A column called completion might mean course completion, application completion, survey completion, or program completion.


Coverage
Coverage asks who or what appears in the data.
Ask:

What population is included?
What population is excluded?
Are there geographic limits?
Are there time limits?
Are small groups combined, suppressed, or missing?

Coverage matters because a source can be accurate for the population it includes and still misleading if used for a different population.


Timeliness
Timeliness asks whether the data are current enough for the communication task.
Ask:

When were the data collected?
When were the data published?
How often are they updated?
Is there a lag between the event and the published data?
Does the audience need the latest available data or a stable historical record?

Recent is not always better. For some questions, a complete older dataset may be more useful than a partial current one. But the audience should not be left guessing about timing.


Format and accessibility
Format asks whether you can actually use the data.
Ask:

Is the data available as .csv, .xlsx, API, database table, PDF, image, or webpage?
Can it be downloaded without copying and pasting by hand?
Is the file readable by R or another tool?
Are column names and formats consistent?
Is the dataset too large or complex for the assignment scope?

PDF tables and screenshots may be useful for reading, but they are often poor formats for analysis. A clean .csv or documented API is usually easier to use.


License and terms of use
License asks what you are allowed to do with the data.
Ask:

Is the data public domain, openly licensed, restricted, or unclear?
Are attribution or citation required?
Are there limits on redistribution?
Are there privacy or confidentiality rules?
Are there terms of use for an API or portal?







WarningPublic does not mean permissionless



Data can be visible online and still have terms of use, attribution requirements, privacy concerns, or ethical limits. Always check the source page and documentation before reusing or republishing data.




Provenance
Provenance means the history of the data: where it came from, how it moved, and how it changed.
For a course project, a provenance note should answer:

Where did the data come from?
Who created or maintains it?
When did you access it?
What version, year, or release did you use?
What file did you download?
What changes did you make before analysis?

Provenance is part of reproducibility. If someone cannot trace your source, they cannot fully evaluate your claim.
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
text:
4.6 Source fit and claim strength
A data source does not support every claim equally.







Claim Type
Source Needs




Descriptive
Clear population, measure, time frame, and definitions


Comparative
Same definitions across groups, fair comparison groups, and relevant denominators


Associational
Variables measured for the same units or time periods, with attention to confounding


Causal
Strong research design, not only a simple comparison


Predictive
Data suitable for forecasting, with enough history and validation


Evaluative
Evidence plus a stated criterion for what counts as good, bad, effective, or sufficient



The source and claim must match. If the source is a one-time survey, be careful with trend claims. If the source is administrative records, be careful with claims about attitudes or motivations. If the source is observational, be careful with causal language.






ExampleExample 4.2: Source fit



A city dashboard reports the number of pothole repair requests submitted each month.
This source may support:

Reported pothole repair requests increased from March to April.

It may not support:

Potholes increased from March to April.

The dashboard counts requests, not all potholes. The difference matters.
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
text:
4.7 A data source note
For this course, a data source note is a short record of what you found and how you evaluated it.
Use this template:
## Data Source Note

**Source title:** 

**Source owner or organization:**

The note does not need to be long. It needs to make your source judgment visible.
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
text:
4.8 Example source note






ExampleExample 4.3: Draft data source note



Source title: County unemployment rate data
Source owner or organization: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics
Link or location: BLS data tools or public data API
Date accessed: August 22, 2026
Data format: Online table, downloadable data, or API
Population or coverage: Labor force data by geographic area
Time period: Monthly or annual series, depending on the selected table
Key variables or measures: Unemployment rate, labor force, employment, unemployment
Documentation available: BLS series documentation and API/data tool notes
License or terms of use: Public source; still cite BLS and follow portal guidance
Possible audience: Local policymakers or community members
Possible claim: The county unemployment rate changed from one month to another.
Important limitation: Month-to-month changes may need seasonal context, revision notes, and comparison to state or national patterns.
AI use or verification note: AI could help draft plain-language explanations, but source links, definitions, and the final claim must be checked against BLS documentation.

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
section: 4.9 Using AI to find and evaluate sources
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
text:
4.10 Common problems to watch for
These problems are common enough that you should check for them before writing a claim.







Problem
Why It Matters




The source has data but no documentation
You may not know what the variables mean


The source measures a proxy
Your claim may name something the data do not directly measure


The time period is unclear
The audience cannot interpret timing or trend


The denominator is missing
Counts may look large or small without context


The data are aggregated
Group-level data may not support individual-level claims


Categories changed over time
Trend comparisons may be unfair


Missing values are not explained
Summaries may be biased or incomplete


The license is unclear
Reuse may be restricted


The file was modified before you received it
Provenance may be incomplete



Finding one of these problems does not always mean you cannot use the source. It means your claim and caveat need to reflect the limit.
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
text:
4.11 Public data sources
Public data portals can be useful starting points. They are not a substitute for source evaluation.
Examples of official public data portals include:

Data.gov, the U.S. government’s open data catalog.
data.census.gov, the U.S. Census Bureau’s data platform.
BLS data tools and BLS Public Data API, which provide access to Bureau of Labor Statistics data.
NCES IPEDS Use the Data, which provides access to postsecondary education data submitted to NCES.

When using any portal, move from the portal record to the documentation. The search result is not enough.
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
text:
4.12 Practical workflow
Use this workflow before starting a data memo:

Write a source-seeking question.
Search likely source owners and public portals.
Open the source page, not only a search result.
Download or bookmark the documentation.
Identify the population, time period, variables, and format.
Check license, terms of use, and citation guidance.
Write a data source note.
Draft only claims that the source can support.
Record any AI help and verification.

This workflow is slower than grabbing the first spreadsheet you find. It is also how you avoid building a polished message on weak evidence.
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
text:
4.13 Recap








Keyword
Definition




Data source
The data file plus the documentation, metadata, ownership, license, and context needed to understand it.


Documentation
Explanation of how the data were collected, what they include, and how they should be interpreted.


Metadata
Information about the dataset, such as owner, title, date, format, license, and update schedule.


Data dictionary
A guide to variables, definitions, units, categories, and codes.


Coverage
The people, places, events, time periods, or units included in the data.


License
The rules or permissions for using, sharing, or republishing the data.


Provenance
The history of where the data came from, when it was accessed, and how it changed.


Source fit
The match between the data source and the claim, audience, and communication task.
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources
text:
4.14 Check your understanding






NoteProblems






Why is a data file alone usually not enough for responsible data communication?
What is the difference between a data dictionary and metadata?
A dashboard reports the number of pothole repair requests submitted each month. Why is “potholes increased” a stronger claim than the source may support?
Name three things you should record in a data source note.
Why does licensing matter even when data are publicly visible online?
Give one useful way to use AI while searching for data sources and one thing you must verify yourself.
Match each term to the best description:

Provenance
Coverage
Source fit
License

Descriptions:

The match between the data source and the claim or communication task.
The history of where the data came from and how it changed.
The rules or permissions for using and sharing the data.
The people, places, events, or time periods included in the data.











TipSolutions






A data file alone usually does not explain where the data came from, what population is included, how variables are defined, how missing values are coded, what time period is covered, or what use restrictions apply. Without that context, it is easy to misinterpret the source.
A data dictionary explains variables: names, definitions, units, categories, and codes. Metadata describes the dataset as a whole: title, owner, date, format, license, update schedule, and other source information.
The dashboard counts repair requests, not all potholes. Requests can change because of reporting behavior, outreach, weather, staffing, or app use. “Repair requests increased” fits the source better than “potholes increased.”
Answers will vary. Good items include source title, owner, link, date accessed, data format, population or coverage, time period, key variables, documentation, license, possible claim, limitation, and AI verification note.
Public visibility does not automatically mean unrestricted reuse. The source may require attribution, limit redistribution, restrict commercial use, include privacy rules, or have terms of use for an API or portal.
AI could help brainstorm search terms, identify likely source owners, summarize documentation you provide, or draft questions to ask about a dataset. You must still verify that the source exists, open the source page, read the documentation, check license or terms, and make sure the source supports the claim.
a-2. b-4. c-1. d-3.
crumbs: 4  Finding and Evaluating Data Sources

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
5.1 Why variable meaning matters
Finding a data source is only the beginning. Before you analyze, summarize, visualize, or communicate from a dataset, you need to understand what the variables mean.
A data dictionary is a guide to the columns, values, units, categories, codes, and limits of a dataset. It helps you move from “I have a file” to “I understand what this file can support.”
In this course, data dictionaries are part of responsible data communication. They help you avoid using a variable incorrectly, making an unsupported claim, or letting AI generate code that appears to work but answers the wrong question.
Datasets often look more self-explanatory than they really are.
Imagine a dataset with these columns:
Those names are short, but they are not enough.
Ask:
The dataset may import into R without errors. The problem is not whether the file opens. The problem is whether the values mean what you think they mean.
crumbs: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
id
term
visits
complete
score
status
group



What kind of id is this?
Does term mean semester, academic year, or payment period?
Does visits count scheduled appointments, completed appointments, or unique days?
Does complete mean a completed course, completed survey, completed appointment, or completed degree?
What scale is score measured on?
What values can status take?
What does group refer to?








WarningDo not trust variable names alone



A variable name is a clue, not a definition. Before using a variable in a claim, check the documentation, codebook, or source notes that explain what the variable actually means.
crumbs: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
5.2 What a data dictionary includes
A useful data dictionary usually includes:

variable name;
plain-language definition;
data type;
unit of measurement;
allowed values or categories;
missing value rules;
source or collection method;
notes about limitations or interpretation.

Here is a basic structure:







Field
Meaning




Variable name
The exact column name in the dataset


Definition
What the variable means in ordinary language


Type
Numeric, character, date, logical, categorical, identifier, etc.


Unit
Dollars, years, visits, percent, points, miles, minutes, etc.


Allowed values
Valid categories, codes, ranges, or levels


Missing values
How missing, unknown, skipped, or not applicable values appear


Notes
Warnings, source details, or interpretation limits



You do not need a perfect dictionary before you begin exploring a dataset. But you do need enough variable meaning to avoid making careless claims.
crumbs: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
section: 5.3 Data type is not the same as meaning
text:
5.3 Data type is not the same as meaning
Data type tells software how values are stored. Meaning tells humans what values represent.








Variable
Possible Data Type
Meaning Question




age
numeric
Age at what date? In years or months? Self-reported or official record?


zip
character
Postal code, not a number to average


grade
numeric or character
Course grade, letter grade, exam score, or grade level?


date
date
Date of event, entry, publication, or update?


status
categorical
What are the valid statuses and how are they assigned?


id
character
Person, record, institution, transaction, or anonymized unit?



A common mistake is to let software type drive interpretation. For example, ZIP codes may be made of digits, but they are identifiers, not quantities. Averaging ZIP codes would be meaningless.






ExampleExample 5.1: Type versus meaning



Suppose a dataset has a column called student_id.
R may store this column as numeric because it contains digits. That does not mean you should calculate the mean of student IDs. The column identifies records. It is not a measurement.
The data type helps software. The definition helps communication.
crumbs: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
5.4 Units
Units tell the reader what a number represents.
Without units, numbers can be ambiguous.







Value
Possible Meanings




12
12 students, 12 percent, 12 visits, 12 weeks, 12 dollars, 12 points


0.82
82%, 0.82 points, 0.82 probability, 0.82 dollars


45
45 minutes, 45 years, 45 responses, 45 miles



Units belong in the data dictionary and often in the final communication.
Weak:

The average was 42.

Better:

The average appointment length was 42 minutes.

Better still:

Among completed tutoring appointments in Spring 2027, the average appointment length was 42 minutes.

The final version includes the measure, unit, population, and time frame.

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
5.5 Categories and codes
Many variables use categories or codes.
Examples:








Variable
Possible Values
Needed Definition




status
C, N, R
What does each code mean?


class_year
first-year, sophomore, junior, senior
How are transfer students coded?


appointment_type
drop-in, scheduled, group
Can one visit have more than one type?


response
1, 2, 3, 4, 5
What question was asked and what do the numbers mean?


race_ethnicity
multiple categories
Are categories self-reported, administrative, combined, or suppressed?



Categories need definitions because category names can carry assumptions.






NoteCodes must be decoded before communication



Do not write to an audience using unexplained internal codes. Translate codes into meaningful labels, and keep the original coding rules in your data dictionary or notes.

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
5.6 Missing values
Missing values are not all the same.
A blank cell could mean:

the question was skipped;
the value was not applicable;
the data were not collected;
the value was suppressed for privacy;
the value failed a quality check;
the source owner has not updated it yet;
the answer was refused;
the student or record was not in the system.

These meanings can lead to different communication choices.



Missing Code
Possible Meaning




blank
No entry, unknown, skipped, or import issue


NA
Missing or not available


N/A
Not applicable


999
Missing, unknown, refused, or legacy code


-1
Missing, not asked, or special system value


suppressed
Hidden because of privacy, small counts, or policy



Before summarizing a variable, ask how missing values are coded and whether they should be included, excluded, recoded, or described.






ExampleExample 5.2: Missing value meaning



Suppose a survey variable records weekly study hours.
If a blank response means “student skipped the question,” excluding blanks may be reasonable but should be noted.
If a blank response means “student was not asked the question,” the missingness may depend on survey version.
If 999 means “prefer not to answer,” treating 999 as 999 hours would destroy the summary.

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
5.7 Measurement limits
Variables are often imperfect measures of the ideas we care about.








Idea We Care About
Possible Variable
Measurement Limit




Academic engagement
Tutoring visits
Visits do not capture studying, office hours, peer support, or motivation


Learning
Exam score
Scores reflect test design, preparation, timing, and grading choices


Community concern
Complaint reports
Reports depend on awareness, access, and willingness to complain


Health access
Appointment wait time
Wait time may miss cost, transportation, insurance, or trust


Economic well-being
Household income
Income may not capture wealth, debt, costs, or household size



This does not mean the variable is useless. It means the claim should match the measure.
If your variable measures tutoring visits, say “tutoring visits” rather than “student motivation.” If your variable measures complaint reports, say “reported complaints” rather than “all problems.”

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
5.8 A data dictionary in Quarto
For a small course project, a data dictionary can be a markdown table in your .qmd file.
## Data Dictionary

| Variable | Definition | Type | Unit or Values | Missing Values | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| student_key | Anonymous student record identifier | character | Unique ID | none expected | Not a measurement |
| visits | Completed tutoring visits during the semester | numeric | count of visits | blank means no record | Does not include canceled appointments |
| course_grade | Final course grade | numeric | points from 0 to 100 | blank if no final grade | Does not prove tutoring caused grade |
| appointment_type | Type of tutoring appointment | categorical | scheduled, drop-in, group | blank if no visit | Categories may overlap in some systems |
For a larger project, a separate .csv or spreadsheet may be easier to maintain.
The important habit is the same: define variables before making claims from them.

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
5.9 Building a question list
A data dictionary often reveals things you still do not know.
That is useful.
A question list is a short list of issues that need clarification before analysis or communication.
Examples:

Does visits count scheduled appointments or completed appointments?
Are canceled appointments included?
Is course_grade a final grade or current grade at the time of export?
Are missing grades missing because students withdrew?
Are transfer students included in class_year?
Did the definition of status change between semesters?
Is the file one row per student, one row per visit, or one row per course?

A good question list protects you from pretending to know more than you do.






TipQuestion lists are productive



Finding unanswered questions is not failure. It is evidence that you are reading the data carefully.

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
5.10 Row meaning
A data dictionary should also clarify what one row represents.
This is sometimes called the unit of observation.







One Row Represents
Example Claim




One student
“In this file, 38% of students visited tutoring at least once.”


One tutoring visit
“Most visits occurred during the two weeks before midterms.”


One course section
“Introductory sections had higher tutoring use than advanced sections.”


One institution
“Enrollment varied across institutions.”


One county-month
“Unemployment rates changed across months and counties.”



If you misunderstand the row meaning, your summaries may be wrong.
For example, if a file has one row per visit, counting rows does not count students. One student with five visits appears five times.

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
section: 5.11 Joining variable meaning to audience and claim
text:
5.11 Joining variable meaning to audience and claim
Variable meaning is not only a technical issue. It affects communication.
Before using a variable in a message, ask:

Would the audience understand the variable name?
Does the variable directly measure the idea in the claim?
What unit or category label needs to be explained?
What missing values could affect the summary?
What caveat should appear near the claim?







ExampleExample 5.3: Revising a claim using variable meaning



Original claim:

Students who used tutoring were more motivated.

Source variable:

visits: count of completed tutoring visits during Spring 2027.

Better claim:

In Spring 2027, students with at least one completed tutoring visit used the tutoring center more than students with no recorded visits.

Even better, if paired with grade data:

In Spring 2027, students with at least one completed tutoring visit had higher average course grades than students with no recorded visits, but the data do not show whether tutoring caused the difference.

The better claims stay closer to the variables.

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
5.13 Common problems to watch for
These problems often appear when students begin working with real datasets.







Problem
Why It Matters




Variable name is unclear
You may make the wrong claim


Unit is missing
The number cannot be interpreted


Categories are coded
The audience will not understand raw codes


Missing values are undocumented
Summaries may be wrong


Row meaning is unclear
Counts and percentages may use the wrong denominator


Date variable is ambiguous
Timing and trend claims may be wrong


Identifier is treated as a number
Software may allow meaningless summaries


Proxy measure is overstated
The claim may name an idea the variable does not directly measure


Definitions changed over time
Comparisons may be unfair



Most of these problems can be handled if they are documented. They become dangerous when they are ignored.

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
5.14 Practical workflow
Use this workflow before cleaning or summarizing a dataset:

Identify what one row represents.
List the variables you expect to use.
Find or create definitions for those variables.
Record data type, unit, categories, and allowed values.
Identify missing value codes.
Write notes about measurement limits.
Create a question list for unclear items.
Draft only claims that match the variable definitions.
Record any AI help and how you verified it.

This workflow slows you down at the start. It saves time later because you will make fewer incorrect summaries and fewer misleading claims.

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
5.15 Recap








Keyword
Definition




Data dictionary
A guide to variables, definitions, units, categories, missing values, and notes.


Variable
A column or field in a dataset that records a measure, category, identifier, date, or other value.


Data type
How software stores a value, such as numeric, character, date, logical, or categorical.


Unit
What a number represents, such as dollars, minutes, visits, percent, or points.


Category
A named group or level, such as scheduled, drop-in, first-year, or completed.


Missing value
A blank, code, or marker showing that a value is unavailable, unknown, not applicable, suppressed, or not collected.


Measurement limit
A boundary on what a variable can tell us.


Unit of observation
What one row in the dataset represents.


Question list
A list of unclear items that must be resolved before analysis or communication.

title: 5  Data Dictionaries and Variable Meaning
text:
5.16 Check your understanding






NoteProblems






Why is a variable name not the same thing as a definition?
What is the difference between data type and variable meaning?
Why should ZIP code usually be treated as an identifier or category rather than a numeric measurement?
A column called visits appears in a tutoring dataset. Name two questions you should ask before using it in a claim.
Why can missing value codes such as 999 or -1 create problems?
What does unit of observation mean?
Explain why “tutoring visits” may be a poor direct measure of “student motivation.”
Give one useful AI task for building a data dictionary and one thing you must verify yourself.
Match each term to the best description:

Unit
Missing value
Data dictionary
Unit of observation

Descriptions:

What one row in the dataset represents.
A guide to variables, definitions, units, categories, missing values, and notes.
A marker showing that a value is unavailable, unknown, not applicable, suppressed, or not collected.
What a number represents, such as dollars, minutes, visits, percent, or points.











TipSolutions






A variable name is only a label. It may be short, vague, or based on internal system language. A definition explains what the variable actually measures or records.
Data type tells software how a value is stored, such as numeric, character, date, logical, or categorical. Variable meaning tells humans what the value represents.
ZIP codes may contain digits, but they identify geographic areas. Averaging or adding ZIP codes would not produce a meaningful quantity.
Answers will vary. Good questions include: Does visits count scheduled or completed visits? Does it count unique students, total visits, or visit days? Are canceled appointments included? What time period is covered? Are missing values possible?
If missing value codes are treated as real values, summaries can be badly distorted. For example, treating 999 as 999 hours or -1 as a real score would produce incorrect averages and misleading claims.
Unit of observation means what one row represents, such as one student, one visit, one course section, one institution, or one county-month.
Tutoring visits measure recorded use of tutoring, not motivation directly. Visits may reflect availability, scheduling, course requirements, awareness of services, transportation, or other factors.
AI could help format a data dictionary table, suggest questions for unclear variables, or draft audience-friendly labels from definitions you provide. You must verify definitions, categories, units, missing value rules, and row meaning against source documentation.
a-4. b-3. c-2. d-1.
